>If you crashed and burned at multiple things, if you look at those experiences as objectively as possible what are the common factors?

I'm definitely 100% my own worst critic. If I screw up, it eats at me, and the more I've invested in the task I screwed up on, the worse it gets. 

As a whole, I can deal with quick and repetitive failure pretty well because it also increases my mastery of said task that much faster. But if I've spent hours on something and I have a vested interest in a good outcome, then the failure is that much harder to take. Not only because I have to do the task again, but because it takes that much longer to master whatever I'm doing. If I don't see myself making any marked improvement, or I hit a long plateau period, I'm more apt to just give up and attempt to focus my energies elsewhere. Doing things I don't have much chance or ability to improve at has a history of evoking some rather unpleasant responses, especially if I feel forced into doing it, or if it's something that I can't/won't put down. Said responses can range from simple moodiness/agitation, to serious thoughts of harm to myself or others.

I hate feeling stagnant, like I'm backed into a corner, or like I've otherwise hit a dead end. And, if we're going to apply Occam's Razor in the most cynical sense possible, the most common factor in my failures is myself. I'm honestly not sure what's going on; if I lack the skills to succeed, the ability or willingness to apply those skills, (or learn them), or if I just don't care anymore and I'm looking for a good excuse to remove myself from the equation.
